title: Greetings & basics
description: Say hello and goodbye, ask how someone is, thank people and give simple answers.

guide.title: Hello and goodbye
guide.text:
Bengali has no everyday 'good morning' or 'good afternoon'. One greeting serves all day, and the same word is used when you leave.

নমস্কার (nomoshkaar) is the usual greeting in West Bengal and among Hindus, often said with the palms together. Muslims, and most people in Bangladesh, greet with আসসালামু আলাইকুম (aassaalaamu aalaaikum); the reply is ওয়ালাইকুম আসসালাম. With friends, people skip the greeting altogether and go straight to 'how are you?'.

শুভ রাত্রি (good night) and শুভ সকাল (good morning) exist, but they are translations of the English phrases: you will see them in messages and hear them on television more than in the street.

When leaving, a Bengali does not say 'I am going' - that sounds unlucky. You say আসি (aashi), literally 'I come', meaning 'I'll be back'.

guide.title: How are you?
guide.text:
The question is 'you how are?': আপনি কেমন আছেন? The verb comes last, as it always does in Bengali. The answer simply swaps in 'I' and changes the verb ending: আমি ভালো আছি, 'I well am'.

Notice the two endings: আছেন (aachhen) goes with আপনি, the polite 'you'; আছি (aachhi) goes with আমি, 'I'. Bengali verbs change with the person and with the level of respect, but never for gender or for singular and plural.

Bengali has three words for 'you'. This course uses the polite আপনি (aapni) until the unit on pronouns; it is the right choice for any adult you do not know well. To a friend you would say তুমি কেমন আছ? (tumi kemon aachho).

The e in কেমন is the open sound of the a in 'cat'.

guide.title: Thank you, sorry, okay
guide.text:
ধন্যবাদ (dhonnobaad) means 'thank you', but it is more formal than the English word and used far less: between friends and family, thanks are shown with a smile or a nod, and saying ধন্যবাদ for every small thing sounds distant. Use it freely with strangers, in shops and in offices. Spelling trap: the ন্য is said as a long n - dhon-no-baad.

মাফ করবেন (maaph korben) is literally 'you will forgive': it covers both 'sorry' and 'excuse me'.

ঠিক আছে (thik aachhe), 'it is right', is the universal 'okay', 'fine', 'all right'.

হ্যাঁ (hyaan) is 'yes' and না (naa) is 'no'. The vowel of হ্যাঁ is the a of 'cat', said through the nose.

phrases.note: Works at any time of day, for both hello and goodbye. The usual greeting in West Bengal.
The everyday greeting among Muslims and throughout Bangladesh. Reply: ওয়ালাইকুম আসসালাম (owaalaaikum aassaalaam).
Polite form. Bengali verbs do not change for gender.
In conversation the আমি is usually dropped: ভালো আছি।
The written ন্য is pronounced as a doubled 'nn'. More formal than English 'thanks'.
The vowel is like the 'a' in English 'cat', nasalised.
The same word placed after a verb means 'not'.
How a guest is welcomed. The ending -un is the polite command.
The polite way to take your leave: you say 'I come', never 'I go'.
Rather formal; modelled on the English phrase.
